<!-- README.md -->

# autocomplete: tab completion and command snippets for bash and zsh

**Fast tab completion, plus ready-made command snippets on `@<TAB>`, for the bash that ships
with macOS (`/bin/bash` 3.2), any newer bash, and zsh. One small C binary, no shell scripts, no dependencies.**

It does two things:

- **Tab completion** for the commands you type every day: subcommands, flags with
  descriptions, and live values such as git branches, docker networks and make targets.
- **Snippets**: type a command, then `@<TAB>`, and pick a complete, working command line.
  No more looking up the curl flags for posting JSON or how to make a tarball.

```console
$ git checkout fe<TAB>
$ git checkout feature/login

$ docker run --network <TAB>
bridge   host   none   my_app_default

$ tar @<TAB>
📌 @c  -- tar -czf backup.tar.gz project/              📚 create a gzip archive of a folder
📌 @x  -- tar -xzf backup.tar.gz                       📚 extract a gzip archive here
📌 @t  -- tar -tzf backup.tar.gz                       📚 list the contents without extracting
🔥 @d  -- tar -xzf backup.tar.gz -C /tmp/out           📚 extract into another directory
🔥 @j  -- tar -cJf backup.tar.xz project/              📚 create an xz archive
...
$ tar @x<TAB>
$ tar -xzf backup.tar.gz
```

You don't need Homebrew bash or the `bash-completion` package. Pressing TAB runs no
shell code, and new terminals open as fast as before. zsh works too, with the same specs
([zsh](docs/installation.md#zsh)).

## Installation

macOS (Apple silicon, Intel) and Linux (x86_64, arm64). Works with bash 3.2 or newer, and
zsh. No sudo: installs to `~/.local` and adds `eval "$(autocomplete bash)"` to `~/.bashrc`
(and `eval "$(autocomplete zsh)"` to `~/.zshrc` when you use zsh).

```sh
curl -fsSL https://github.com/hza/autocomplete/releases/latest/download/install.sh | sh
```

or with `wget`:

```sh
wget -qO- https://github.com/hza/autocomplete/releases/latest/download/install.sh | sh
```

Open a new terminal and press TAB after `git`, `docker` or `make`. For manual download,
building from source, install options and uninstalling, see
[Installation options](docs/installation.md).

## Snippets

Most completion tools help you spell a flag you already know. Snippets help when you don't
remember which flags you need. Type `@` right after the command and press TAB: each snippet
is a working command with a short key and a one-line explanation. `@key<TAB>` inserts it,
ready to edit. 📌 marks the most used ones, which are listed first. A plain TAB never shows
snippets, so it keeps completing files, hosts and flags as usual.

About 135 commands have snippets. Highlights:

- **port** (MacPorts): selfupdate, upgrade outdated, leaves, reclaim, reverse dependencies
- **curl**, **wget**: POST JSON or form data, uploads, headers only, redirects, resuming
- **ps**, **lsof**: top CPU/memory processes, who listens on a port, open files of a process
- **find**, **grep**: recently changed files, large files, recursive search with excludes
- **tar**, **zip**, **unzip**, **unrar**, **gzip**, **xz**, **bzip2**: create, extract, list,
  exclude folders, zip without macOS junk, passwords, split archives, `.app` bundles
- **ssh**: port forwarding, jump hosts, SOCKS proxy, remote commands
- **jq**: pretty-print, pick and filter fields, CSV, shell variables
- **brew**: dependency trees, reverse dependencies, leaves, cleanup, Brewfile backup
- **docker**: `run`, `exec`, the `prune` commands, `compose config`
- **kubectl**, **rsync**, **ffmpeg**, **openssl**, **jfr** and many more
- macOS tools: **defaults** (hidden Finder, Dock and screenshot settings), **sips** (resize,
  convert HEIC), **mdfind**, **pbcopy**, **say**, **duti**
- Shell keywords **for**, **while**, **until**, **case**, **if**: practical one-liners
  (`if git <TAB>` still completes git)

Add your own with a `snippets:` list in any spec ([format](docs/writing-specs.md)).

bash-completion, zsh and fish complete flags and values only. Cheat-sheet tools like
[navi](https://github.com/denisidoro/navi) or [tldr](https://tldr.sh) show examples, but in
a separate command, not at the prompt you're already typing on.

## Completion

**Bundled commands** (about 150):

- **Version control and build:** git, gh, make, mvn, gradle, cargo, go, swift, pod, fastlane
- **Languages and packages:** python, pip, pyenv, node, npm, npx, yarn, pnpm, bun, bunx,
  java, jfr, rbenv, asdf, nvm
- **Containers and cloud:** docker, colima, orbctl, kubectl, kubectx, kubens, k9s, helm,
  minikube, kind, terraform, pulumi, ansible, aws, az, gcloud, doctl, flyctl, vercel
- **Databases:** psql, pg_dump, mysql, mysqldump, redis-cli, sqlite3
- **Network:** ssh, scp, curl, wget, rsync, openssl, dig, nc, tcpdump
- **Files and text:** find, grep, rg, sed, awk, diff, patch, jq, bat, fzf, tar, zip, unzip,
  unrar, gzip, xz, bzip2, compress (and their decompressors)
- **Processes:** ps, kill, pkill, killall, lsof, tmux
- **macOS:** port (MacPorts), brew, mas, open, defaults, launchctl, diskutil, pmset,
  networksetup, security, codesign, xcrun, plutil, hdiutil, spctl, xattr, softwareupdate,
  tccutil, scutil, mdutil, mdfind, mdls, osascript, shortcuts, dscl, log, system_profiler,
  ditto, textutil, sips, screencapture, say, afplay, qlmanage, caffeinate, pbcopy, pbpaste,
  duti, profiles, sw_vers, nettop, fs_usage
- **Other:** code (VS Code), claude (Claude Code), ffmpeg, pngquant, jpegtran, man, help, and
  `autocomplete` itself

**Live values** from your environment, for example:

- git: branches, tags, remotes, stashes, changed files, your aliases
- docker: containers, images, networks, volumes
- kubectl: namespaces, contexts, pods, nodes, resource types
- make: targets and variables, with descriptions from `## text` or the comment above each
  target (honors `-C dir` and `-f file`)
- npm, yarn, pnpm, bun, node: `package.json` scripts and dependencies; npx, bunx: binaries
  in `node_modules/.bin`
- mvn: profiles, modules and plugin goals from `pom.xml`
- ssh, scp: hosts from `~/.ssh/config` and `known_hosts` (`scp gr<TAB>` → `grafana:`)
- java: source files that declare `main` (`java <TAB>`); python: modules for `-m`
  (`python3 -m http<TAB>` → `http.server`)
- aws, az, gcloud: profiles, subscriptions, projects, regions, buckets
- gh: pull requests, issues, workflow runs, releases; helm: releases and charts;
  terraform: resources from state
- kill, killall, pkill: running processes; say: voices; open: app names and bundle ids
- duti: file extensions, app bundle ids (also by app name: `duti -s Preview<TAB>`) and every
  UTI known to the system, read live from LaunchServices

**More:**

- Descriptions next to subcommands and flags (`git stash <TAB>` →
  `pop  -- Apply a stash and remove it`).
- Commands with hundreds of flags, like curl and wget, are grouped to fit your screen.
- `sudo`, `env`, `time` and `xargs` complete the command after them
  (`sudo git chec<TAB>` → `checkout`).
- Handles `--flag=value`, `image:tag`, quoted words and file names with spaces.
- Shell aliases complete like the command they wrap (`autocomplete alias kubectl k`).
- Any other command: generate a spec from its man page or `--help` output, or hand Go/cobra
  programs over to their own completion ([details](docs/generated-specs.md)). With
  `autocomplete bash --man`, every command with a man page completes its flags automatically.
- Your own commands: write a small YAML file, no rebuild ([how](docs/adding-commands.md)).

## Commands

| Command | Description |
|---|---|
| `autocomplete bash [--man]` | Print the init script (use with `eval`). `--man` also registers every command in `$PATH` that has a man page and no spec; its flags are read from the man page on first TAB and [cached](docs/cache.md#man-page-specs). |
| `autocomplete zsh [--man]` | Same for zsh: defines one completion function and registers it with `compdef` (loads `compinit` if needed). |
| `autocomplete list [--user] [--paths] [--tsv]` | List commands that have a spec, with descriptions. `--user`: only your specs in `~/.config/autocomplete`. `--paths`: show which spec file is used. `--tsv`: `NAME<TAB>DESCRIPTION` for scripts. Your specs are tagged `[override]`, `[added]` or `[alias -> CMD]`, plus `generated: …` and `update: NEW > OLD` when the shipped spec is newer. |
| `autocomplete manage` | Same as `list --user`. |
| `autocomplete add [--force] [--from cobra\|man\|help] CMD...` | Write `~/.config/autocomplete/CMD.yaml` from the first source that works: cobra, man page, `CMD --help`. |
| `autocomplete edit NAME` | Edit your copy of a spec in `$VISUAL`/`$EDITOR`/`vi`, copying the shipped one first if needed. Validates after saving; an unchanged copy is removed. |
| `autocomplete diff [NAME...]` | `diff -u` of your copies against the shipped specs. Exits 1 if any differ. |
| `autocomplete rm [-f] NAME...` | Delete your spec or alias (asks first unless `-f`); the shipped spec is used again. |
| `autocomplete alias [--force] CMD NAME...` | Complete `NAME` like `CMD`. |
| `autocomplete alias --rm NAME...` / `--list` | Remove or list aliases. |
| `autocomplete check FILE` | Validate a spec and print how it was parsed (as JSON). |

## FAQ

### Why another bash completion tool?

macOS still ships bash 3.2 from 2007, and the usual tools have moved on:

- **bash-completion 2.x** requires bash 4.2 or newer.
- **bash-completion 1.3**, the last version for bash 3.2, is unmaintained and loads every
  completion script at startup, so each new terminal opens slowly.
- The common workaround is `brew install bash` and changing your login shell.

autocomplete is built for the bash you already have. It's tested against Apple's `/bin/bash`
and builds with the Xcode Command Line Tools.

### Why is it fast?

bash-completion is written in bash and sources its scripts into every shell. autocomplete
registers its binary with `complete -C`, so each TAB runs compiled C directly: no bash
functions, `sed`/`awk` pipelines or subshells. Shell startup does only the registration;
specs are read when you press TAB.

### Why C and not Rust?

- **Nothing extra to install.** C builds with the Xcode Command Line Tools that most Macs
  already have. Rust needs `rustup` and a toolchain of about 1 GB just to run `make`.
- **Size.** The whole engine, including its own YAML parser, is a ~95 KB binary with no
  dependencies. A Rust "Hello, world!" release build is already ~300 KB, because Rust's
  standard library is built into every program.
- **Startup time.** The binary starts on every TAB, so a small binary that only uses libc keeps
  each completion fast.

### Is there a Homebrew package?

No. Homebrew has dropped support for Intel Macs, so I don't support it. Use the install script
above or one of the [other options](docs/installation.md).

### Can I add completion for my own command?

Yes. Write `~/.config/autocomplete/<command>.yaml` describing its subcommands, flags and
values. See [Adding your own commands](docs/adding-commands.md).

<!-- docs/installation.md -->

# Installation options

The quickest way to install is the install script from the [README](../README.md#installation).
This page covers the script's options and the other ways to set autocomplete up.

Prebuilt binaries are published for macOS (Apple silicon and Intel) and Linux (x86_64, arm64).
You need bash 3.2 (the macOS `/bin/bash`) or any newer bash, or zsh ([zsh](#zsh)).

## Install script options

Set `PREFIX=/usr/local`, `PROFILE=~/.bash_profile`, `ZPROFILE=~/.zprofile` or `VERSION=v0.1.0` for `sh` to change the
defaults (e.g. `... | PREFIX=$HOME/bin sh`). The script verifies the download's SHA-256
checksum. Uninstall with `... | sh -s -- --uninstall` (same `PREFIX`/`PROFILE`/`ZPROFILE`).

## Manual download

Pick the tarball for your system (`darwin-arm64`, `darwin-x86_64`,
`linux-x86_64`, `linux-arm64`; Linux binaries are static and run on any distro):

```sh
t=darwin-arm64
curl -fLO https://github.com/hza/autocomplete/releases/latest/download/autocomplete-$t.tar.gz
mkdir -p ~/.local && tar -xzf autocomplete-$t.tar.gz -C ~/.local   # bin/ + share/autocomplete/
echo 'eval "$(~/.local/bin/autocomplete bash)"' >> ~/.bashrc
```

The binary finds its specs in `../share/autocomplete` next to `bin/`, so keep the two together.

## From source

Requires the Xcode Command Line Tools (`xcode-select --install`) on macOS, or gcc/clang and
make on Linux.

```sh
git clone https://github.com/hza/autocomplete.git
cd autocomplete
make install
```

`make install`:

- installs the binary to `/usr/local/bin/autocomplete`,
- installs the bundled specs to `/usr/local/share/autocomplete/`,
- adds `eval "$(autocomplete bash)"` to `~/.bashrc`, unless it's already there,
- adds `eval "$(autocomplete zsh)"` to `~/.zshrc` when that file exists or your login shell
  is zsh.

Open a new terminal (or run `source ~/.bashrc`) and press TAB after `docker`, `git` or `make`.

> macOS Terminal starts login shells, which read `~/.bash_profile`, not `~/.bashrc`.
> `make install` warns if your `~/.bash_profile` doesn't load `~/.bashrc`; add
> `[ -f ~/.bashrc ] && . ~/.bashrc` to it.

Options:

```sh
make install PREFIX=$HOME/.local          # install without sudo (put ~/.local/bin on PATH first)
make install PROFILE=$HOME/.bash_profile  # use a different startup file
make install ZPROFILE=$HOME/.zprofile     # same for zsh
```

If `/usr/local` isn't writable, use `sudo make install`.

## Using it without installing

```sh
make
eval "$(./autocomplete bash)"                     # recommended
source /dev/stdin <<<"$(./autocomplete bash)"     # if you prefer `source`
```

> `source <(autocomplete bash)` does **not** work in bash 3.2. A long-standing bash bug
> makes it silently read nothing. Use one of the forms above.

## zsh

The same binary and specs work in zsh. Add this line to `~/.zshrc` (the installers do it
for you when `~/.zshrc` exists or zsh is your login shell):

```sh
eval "$(autocomplete zsh)"           # or: eval "$(autocomplete zsh --man)"
```

It runs `compinit` if your `~/.zshrc` hasn't already, then registers one completion function
for every command with a spec. That replaces zsh's own completion for those commands (git,
docker, …). Re-run the line after adding a spec.

zsh shows descriptions, groups and menus natively, so a few bash-specific tricks are left out.
Long flag lists aren't folded into `--`, `📌` or `🧩` entries. Snippets work as in bash: `@<TAB>` lists them as `@key  -- command`
without changing the line, and `@key<TAB>`
substitutes that command directly, as in bash. `$VAR`, `~user` and
`user@host` words use zsh's own completion.

## Uninstalling a source install

```sh
make uninstall          # use the same PREFIX / PROFILE you installed with
```

This removes the binary, the bundled specs, their cache files and the exact `eval` line
from your profile. Your own specs in `~/.config/autocomplete` are left untouched.

---

<!-- docs/adding-commands.md -->

# Adding your own commands

Drop a YAML file into `~/.config/autocomplete/`, named after the command:

```yaml
# ~/.config/autocomplete/kubectl.yaml
flags:
  --context: {value: any, description: Name of the kubeconfig context}
commands:
  logs:
    description: Print the logs of a pod    # shown when several commands match
    flags:
      -f: {description: Stream the logs}    # no "value": the flag takes none
    args:
      exec: kubectl get pods -o name | cut -d/ -f2
  apply:
    flags:
      -f: {value: file, description: File to apply}
```

Then run `eval "$(autocomplete bash)"` again (or open a new terminal).

Check the file for mistakes with:

```sh
autocomplete check ~/.config/autocomplete/kubectl.yaml
```

Later edits to the file take effect on the next TAB; only adding a *new* command needs the
`eval` step.

## Shell aliases

If you have `alias dk=docker`, give `dk` the docker completions with:

```sh
autocomplete alias docker dk   # ~/.config/autocomplete/dk.yaml -> docker's spec
```

Then re-run the `eval` step. `--force` replaces an existing `dk` spec. Since it's a symlink, edits
to the docker spec apply to `dk` too.

`autocomplete alias --list` shows your aliases (`dk -> docker`). To remove one:
`autocomplete alias --rm dk` (TAB after `--rm` lists your aliases). Only
symlinks are removed, never real specs.

See [Writing specs](writing-specs.md) for the full format: all value types, supported YAML
and where specs are looked up.

---

<!-- docs/writing-specs.md -->

# Writing specs

A *spec* is a YAML file that describes one command. Create
`~/.config/autocomplete/<command>.yaml`, then run `eval "$(autocomplete bash)"` again
(or open a new terminal) so bash picks up the new command. Edits to an existing spec take
effect on the next TAB.

## Example

`~/.config/autocomplete/kubectl.yaml`:

```yaml
flags:
  --namespace: {aliases: [-n], value: {exec: "kubectl get ns -o name | cut -d/ -f2"}, description: Namespace}
  --context: {value: any, description: Name of the kubeconfig context}
  --help: {aliases: [-h], description: Show help}        # no value
commands:
  get:
    commands:           # fixed words are written as subcommands
      pods: {}
      deployments: {}
      services: {}
  logs:
    flags:
      -f: {description: Stream the logs}
      --tail: {value: any, description: Number of lines to show}
    args:
      exec: kubectl get pods -o name | cut -d/ -f2
  apply:
    flags:
      -f: {value: file, description: File to apply}
  help:
    args: "@subcommands"
```

## Spec format

A spec has these optional keys, and `commands` nests the same structure for subcommands:

| Key | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `flags` | Map of flag name → flag (see below) |
| `inherit_flags` | Top level only: `false` when the program accepts its top-level flags only before the subcommand (docker: `docker -D ps` works, `docker ps -D` fails). By default top-level flags are offered after subcommands too (git, mvn). |
| `args` | What positional arguments complete to (a value) |
| `positional` | List of values by position: the 1st positional argument completes to the 1st entry, the 2nd to the 2nd, and so on; past the end of the list, `args` applies. E.g. `git worktree add` uses `[dir, <branches>]` |
| `commands` | Map of subcommand name → spec |
| `description` | One-line summary shown next to this command when several commands match |
| `aliases` | List of other names for this subcommand, e.g. `aliases: [i, add]` under `install`; each is matched like the main name and shown in its description (`install  -- Install a package (🔥 i, add)`); an alias is offered as a candidate only once typed in full |
| `alias_exec` | Shell command printing user-defined aliases of this spec's subcommands, one `name expansion` line each (space or tab between), e.g. git's `git config --get-regexp '^alias\.' \| sed 's/^alias\.//'`. A plain rename (`re = rebase`) is shown in the target's description like a static alias (`rebase -- … (🔥 re)`); others are listed with `🔥 alias: <expansion>` as description; a name defined twice (git: global, then local) takes the last definition; after an alias the line completes as the subcommand it expands to (first non-flag word, alias chains followed). Shell aliases (`!...`) resolve only with a `: git <sub>` hint inside, e.g. `!f() { : git switch ; ... }; f` |
| `bridge` | Top level only: `cobra` hands every completion to the program itself (`CMD __complete …`, Go programs built with cobra); the rest of the spec is ignored. Written by `autocomplete add CMD` |
| `version` | Top level only: `'YYYYMMDD'` date of the last change to a shipped spec (first line). `autocomplete list` shows `[override, update: NEW > OLD]` and `autocomplete edit` warns when your copy in `~/.config/autocomplete` is older than the shipped one (`autocomplete diff NAME` shows the changes). Ignored by completion |
| `generated` | Top level only: `cobra`, `man` or `help`, the source `autocomplete add` wrote the spec from. Ignored by completion; `add --force CMD` regenerates from it |
| `when` | Only list this subcommand if a file in the current directory exists and (optionally) contains a string, e.g. `when: {file: pom.xml, contains: "<artifactId>spotless-maven-plugin</artifactId>"}`. Used for plugin goals that exist only in some projects. A typed command is still recognised either way |
| `snippets` | List of `{key, command, description?, mark?}` (any level), shown on TAB after the command word (on an empty word only when nothing else would be listed, always after `@`) as `📌 @s  -- curl -sS https://api.github.com/zen   📚 quiet GET, errors still shown`. `key` is 1–8 lowercase letters or digits, unique within the list (`@ss` substitutes key `ss`; a prefix matching one key substitutes it, several are listed); pick a mnemonic one, usually one char (when two snippets want the same letter, give it to the more useful one). `mark: pin` marks the most used ones (📌, listed first); `mark` can also be one of the names `bell` 🔔, `bulb` 💡, `calendar` 📅, `chart` 📈, `clock` 🕐, `console` 💻 (snippets that open an interactive session), `eyes` 👀, `fire` 🔥, `globe` 🌐, `key` 🔑, `link` 🔗, `lock` 🔒, `memo` 📝, `package` 📦, `pin` 📌, `pumpkin` 🎃, `rocket` 🚀, `siren` 🚨, `skull` 💀, `star` 🌟, `target` 🎯, `test` 🧪, `whale` 🐳, `1`…`9` 1️⃣…9️⃣ (or the keycap itself: `mark: 1️⃣`), or one emoji used as the icon directly (`mark: 👀`); `autocomplete emoji` lists the names, `autocomplete emoji 🔥` prints `fire` and `autocomplete emoji fire` prints 🔥: a single code point in U+1F300–U+1FAFF, without U+FE0F (e.g. not ❤️), so it is always 2 columns wide; `autocomplete check` rejects others. Unmarked snippets get 🔥. 📌 entries are listed first in both locales (in the C locale only keycap entries come before them), the rest sorted by icon code point (👀 before 🔥); with `LANG=en_US.UTF-8` macOS ignores the other emoji and sorts them by `@key`, keycap entries last (see [troubleshooting](troubleshooting.md)). Typing `@s` and TAB replaces it with the snippet's command after the command name, or the command path for subcommands (`curl @s` → `curl -sS https://api.github.com/zen`; `docker volume prune @x` → `docker volume prune -a -f`); a spec reached through a symlink (`fly.yaml` → `flyctl.yaml`) accepts snippets written with either name; snippets that don't start with the command name (pipelines like `git rev-parse HEAD \| pbcopy`) are only listed. `autocomplete check` fails on missing or duplicate keys. Write them yourself (don't copy text from other projects' docs: their licenses may require attribution); meant for commands whose TAB lists nothing else. |
| `groups` | Map of short-flag letters → `{description?}`, grouping rarely used short flags by meaning. Each key lists the letters of `-x` flags (or `-x` aliases) of this spec (or the top-level one) that are hidden from the list and shown together in one entry: `"Up": {description: proxy}` gives `-📌 Up  -- proxy: (U) Proxy user and password (p) HTTP proxy tunnel (using CONNECT)`. Top-level groups apply at every depth. `autocomplete check` reports letters with no matching flag |

Each flag is a map of optional keys, usually written on one line:

| Key | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `aliases` | Other names of the same flag, e.g. `--version: {aliases: [-v]}`. Key the flag by its long name and list the short ones here. Each name is matched like the key (value, `repeat`, already-typed check) |
| `value` | What the flag's value completes to. Leave it out if the flag takes no value. |
| `description` | One-line summary shown next to the flag when several flags match |
| `repeat` | `true`: the flag may be given several times (`ssh -v -v`). A flag without a `value` that is already on the line isn't offered again unless it has `repeat: true`; flags with a value are always offered |
| `show` | `always`: a frequently used flag, never folded into a group or into `-📌` (see below). `collapsed` (short names only, including a short alias): a rarely used flag, left out of the list and only named in a `📌` entry; still listed when nothing else matches. `default` (or leaving it out): the normal behaviour |

A flag with `aliases` is listed once, under the name that fits what you typed: short names first (`-<TAB>` shows `-d  -- HTTP POST data (🔥 --data)`), long names once the word starts with `--` (`--d<TAB>` shows `--data  -- HTTP POST data (🔥 -d)`). The other names follow as a hint. Inside a `📌` fold the hint is left out. `autocomplete add` writes `-d, --data` style man/help entries this way.

Flags on the top-level spec are offered after any subcommand too. A flag name ending in `=` (e.g. mvn's `'-Dtest=': {}`) is completed without a trailing space, so you can type the value straight after it; give it a `value` to complete that value too (mvn's `-Dspring-boot.run.profiles=` lists `application-<profile>.*` files). Inside an open quote (`-Dx='-Xmx1g -X`) the last space-separated word is completed, so a quoted value can hold several. Quote such keys in YAML.

On a bare `-<TAB>`, if the command has short flags and 15 or more long ones, and the whole list would not fit the screen, only the short ones are listed and the long ones are folded into one entry, `--  -- 256 options: abstract-unix-socket alt-svc …` (as many names as fit). Type `--<TAB>` to list them.

When the flag list is taller than the terminal, flags are grouped by their next letter: `--content-disposition` and `--content-on-error` fall into one `--c  -- connect-timeout content-disposition content-on-error …` entry. Type `--c<TAB>` (no space is added) to list that group; a big group is split again by the following letter. If all flags in a group share a longer prefix, the entry is that prefix: `--no-  -- no-🧩`. In the name list, names sharing a first word are shown once: `sasl-authzid sasl-ir` → `sasl-🧩`. The smallest groups are then shown in full again while the list still fits, so `node --<TAB>` lists its two `--no-` flags directly.

```yaml
flags:
  --rm: {description: Remove the container when it exits}   # takes no value
  --name: {value: any, description: Assign a name}
  -f: {value: file}
  -q: {}                                                     # no value, no description
```

A value can be:

| Value | Completes to |
|---|---|
| *(empty)*, `~`, `null` | nothing |
| `any` | free text, no suggestions |
| `file` / `dir` | paths / directories only; a word like `~ro` lists `~root/`-style home directories |
| `file: "*.json *.yaml"` | files matching one of the space-separated patterns, plus directories to descend into |
| `"@hosts"` | host names from `~/.ssh/config` (`Host` lines without wildcards) and `~/.ssh/known_hosts` (not hashed entries or IP addresses) |
| `"@users"` | login users (not the `_` system accounts), with their full names |
| `"@pids"` | process IDs of your processes, with the program name |
| `"@processes"` | names of your running programs |
| `"@signals"` | signal names: `HUP`, `INT`, `KILL`, … |
| `enum: [json, yaml]` | these fixed words; no command is run |
| `enum: {f: file, d: directory}` | the same, with a description for each (`name:` with nothing after it has none). Quote keys YAML would read as numbers or booleans (`'1'`, `'yes'`). A word ending in `=` gets no space; `suffix` and `nospace` work as for `exec` |
| `exec: <shell command>` | one suggestion per output line; `name<TAB>description` shows the description next to it (e.g. `printf '%s\t%s\n' "$pid" "$name"`); a line ending in `=` (`label=`) gets no space so you can type its value |
| &nbsp;&nbsp;`suffix: ":"` | appended to each suggestion |
| &nbsp;&nbsp;`nospace: true` | don't add a space after accepting it |
| &nbsp;&nbsp;`tree: true` | show `a/b` names as `a/` until you type past the `/`, like paths (e.g. `origin/` for remote branches) |
| &nbsp;&nbsp;`tree: "."` | the same, folding at another separator character (e.g. `com.` for UTIs in duti) |
| &nbsp;&nbsp;`cache: 300` | reuse the output for that many seconds (per command, current directory and, if the command reads `$AUTOCOMPLETE_CUR`, typed word), for slow commands; kept in `~/.cache/autocomplete/exec/` |
| &nbsp;&nbsp;`filter: false` | show every line the command prints, even ones not starting with the typed word (the command filters itself, e.g. duti turns `md` into `net.daringfireball.markdown`) |
| &nbsp;&nbsp;`snippets: true` | the command prints `key<TAB>value<TAB>description` lines (an optional 4th column is the `mark`: an icon name or an emoji), listed like `snippets` (`🔥 @j  -- json   📚 …`); typing `@j` and TAB inserts that value single-quoted (good for templates such as docker `--format`) |
| `"@subcommands"` | the parent command's subcommands (e.g. `git help <TAB>`) |
| `"@command"` | a command from `$PATH`; the words after it are completed with that command's spec (e.g. `sudo`, `xargs`). Words with `=` before the command are skipped (`env FOO=1 git …`), and so is `!` (`if ! git …`). Use it as `args`. |
| `"@make-targets"` | targets of the Makefile, with descriptions (see below) |
| `"@make-variables"` | `NAME=` for each upper-case variable (`A-Z`, `0-9`, `_`) the Makefile assigns, for overrides like `make CC=clang` |
| a list `[a, b]` | everything from each item, combined |

Notes:

- Items in a list are value *types*, not literal words: `[pods, deployments]` looks for
  types named `pods` and `deployments`. To offer fixed words, either list them as
  subcommands (`commands: {pods: {}, deployments: {}}`) or use `enum: [pods, deployments]`.
- Run `autocomplete check <file>` to validate a spec; errors include line numbers.
- Flags defined at the top level are recognised after any subcommand.
- Descriptions appear when more than one command or flag matches:
  ```
  $ git stash <TAB>
  apply   -- Apply a stash, keeping it
  drop    -- Remove a stash
  pop     -- Apply a stash and remove it
  ...
  ```
  They are plain text: bash 3.2 can't display colors in the completion list. Long
  descriptions are cut to fit the terminal width.
- When one list mixes kinds of suggestions (subcommands, files, make targets and
  variables), each line is tagged, since bash sorts the list and can't show section headers.
  Make variables also show the value the Makefile assigns:
  ```
  $ make D<TAB>
  Dockerfile  -- [target] Generate the Dockerfile
  DESTDIR=    -- [var]    Staging root · ?= /tmp/stage
  ```
  On a bare `make <TAB>` the variables are folded into one display-only `📌 vars`
  line listing their names, so targets come first. It is never inserted; type a letter
  (`make C<TAB>`) to list matching variables with their values:
  ```
  $ make <TAB>
  all      -- Build everything
  build
  📌 vars  -- CC PREFIX X
  $ make C<TAB>
  CC=      -- C compiler · ?= cc
  CFLAGS=  -- ?= -O2
  ```
- `"@make-targets"` and `"@make-variables"` read descriptions from the Makefile itself: either `## text` after the
  target or assignment, or the comment lines directly above it (`##` wins if both are present):
  ```make
  # Build the binary
  app: main.c

  test: app  ## Run the test suite
  ```
- `exec` commands run in the current directory, and their errors are discarded.
- For anything longer than a one-liner, put a script next to the spec and run it via
  `$AUTOCOMPLETE_SPEC_DIR`, the directory of the spec being used (symlinks resolved), e.g.
  `exec: 'osascript -l JavaScript "$AUTOCOMPLETE_SPEC_DIR/duti.js" apps'`. If you copy such a spec
  into `~/.config/autocomplete`, copy its script too.
- `exec` commands also get `$AUTOCOMPLETE_CUR`: the word being completed, with shell escapes
  removed (`Visual\ Stu` → `Visual Stu`). Use it with `filter: false` to match by your own rules.
- Values starting with `@` must be quoted.

## Supported YAML

The YAML reader is built into the binary and covers what specs need: indented mappings and
lists, inline `{...}` and `[...]`, single- and double-quoted strings, and `#` comments.
Anchors, tags and multi-line strings (`|`, `>`) are not supported. Indent with spaces, not
tabs.

A `#` after a space starts a comment, even inside an unquoted value. If a command contains
` #`, quote the whole value:

```yaml
exec: "echo 'not # a comment'"
```

## Where specs are looked up

The first match wins, so your own files override the bundled ones:

1. directories in `$AUTOCOMPLETE_SPECS` (colon-separated)
2. `~/.config/autocomplete`
3. `specs/` next to the binary
4. `../share/autocomplete` relative to the binary (where `make install` puts them)

Files must be named `<command>.yaml` or `<command>.yml`. Inside each directory,
specs may be organised into subfolders (up to 4 levels deep): a file directly in
the directory wins over one in a subfolder, and subfolders are searched in
alphabetical order. Helper scripts used by `exec` (see `$AUTOCOMPLETE_SPEC_DIR`)
belong in the same folder as their spec.

The bundled [`specs/`](../specs) are grouped by topic (`vcs/`, `cloud/`, `lang/`,
`build/`, `db/`, `macos/`, `net/`, `shell/`, `tools/`); e.g. `vcs/git.yaml`,
`cloud/docker.yaml`, `lang/npm.yaml` are good real-world examples.

---

<!-- docs/generated-specs.md -->

# Generating specs: man pages, --help, cobra

`autocomplete add CMD...` writes a spec for you into `~/.config/autocomplete/CMD.yaml`,
from the first source that works:

| Source (`--from`) | What it reads |
|---|---|
| `cobra` | the program's own completion, for Go programs built with cobra (kubectl, helm, gh, hugo, ...) |
| `man` | the man page (flags, descriptions, values) |
| `help` | `CMD --help` output, for tools without a man page |

```sh
autocomplete add ps kubectl rsync   # prints each file with the source used, e.g. ".../ps.yaml (man)"
autocomplete add --from help ps     # use only this source
autocomplete add --force ps         # overwrite an existing file
```

The spec records the source it came from as `generated: man` (right after `description`).
`autocomplete add --force CMD` without `--from` regenerates from that same source, so a spec
you once made with `--from help` stays a `--help` spec when you refresh it.

## From man pages

Most system commands (`ps`, `ls`, `grep`, `tar`, `ssh`, ...) document their options in a
man page. autocomplete can read the page and turn it into flag completion with
descriptions, so you don't have to write a spec by hand.

```sh
autocomplete add --from man ps ls grep    # writes ~/.config/autocomplete/ps.yaml, ls.yaml, grep.yaml
autocomplete add --from man --force ps    # overwrite an existing file
```

Every generated spec starts with a `description:` (shown by `autocomplete list`):
the man page's NAME line, the intro paragraph of `--help` output (for cobra programs,
of `CMD --help`), else the `whatis` line (`man -f CMD`). If none is found it is left
empty (`description: ''`) for you to fill in.

The result is an ordinary spec. Open it and fix anything the parser got wrong, or add
live values (see [Writing specs](writing-specs.md)). For example, change `-p`'s value in
`ps.yaml` to list running PIDs:

```yaml
  -p:
    value: {exec: "ps -axo pid= | tr -d ' '"}
```

Open a new terminal (or run `eval "$(autocomplete bash)"` again) so the new command is
registered. After a system update changes a man page, run `autocomplete add --from man --force CMD` to
regenerate the spec (this overwrites your edits).

### What gets extracted

- **Flags**: every option entry in the page, like `-a`, `--text`, or `-A num, --after-context=num`.
- **Descriptions**: the first sentence of each option's text.
- **Values**: a flag takes a value when its entry or the SYNOPSIS shows one (`-O fmt`,
  `[-p pid]`). A value named like a file or path completes files, one named like a
  directory completes directories, and any other value completes nothing.
- **Arguments**: files.

### Limits

- Man pages are free text, so the result is a heuristic. Pages that show example command
  lines at the same indentation as the options (curl, for example) can produce a few extra
  flags.
- Combined short flags like `ls -la` are accepted, but TAB doesn't suggest more letters to
  add to them.
- Values and subcommands are not inferred. Add them by hand to a generated spec.

## From --help

```sh
autocomplete add --from help rsync node
```

Uses the same option parser as `--from man`, on the output of `CMD --help`. On top of that it
reads:

- option lists starting at the left margin (python's `-b     : issue warnings…`);
- the `usage:` line, so a tool whose help is only a synopsis (`[--append] [-e program]`)
  still gets its flags;
- `Commands:` / `Available Commands:` sections, which become subcommands with their
  descriptions. Their own flags are not read: `--from help` never runs `CMD SUB --help`,
  since a subcommand that ignores `--help` would do real work.
- without such a section, one usage block per subcommand (`jfr print [--events <filter>]
  <file>` followed by an indented description line). Each block becomes a subcommand with
  the flags from its brackets, file arguments for `<file>`, and the description.

The command is run with `--help` and stdin from `/dev/null`; don't use it on programs that
might act on an unknown flag.

## From cobra

```sh
autocomplete add --from cobra helm
```

Programs built with Go's cobra library answer `CMD __complete WORDS…` with their own
completions, including live values (helm releases, kube contexts, gh repositories). The
generated spec is just

```yaml
bridge: cobra
```

and every TAB asks the program. File and directory answers, extension filters and
"no space" hints are honoured. `--from cobra` refuses programs that don't answer like cobra.
A program with a bundled spec (kubectl, helm, docker) keeps using the spec unless you
generate one: your `~/.config/autocomplete` file wins.

---

<!-- docs/troubleshooting.md -->

# Troubleshooting

| Problem | What to check |
|---|---|
| Nothing happens on TAB | `complete -p docker` should print `complete -o nospace -o bashdefault -C '/path/to/autocomplete _complete' docker`. If not, the `eval` line didn't run; open a new terminal or check your profile. |
| Works in some terminals (e.g. inside `mc`) but not in new Terminal.app windows or tabs | Terminal.app starts login shells, which read `~/.bash_profile` and not `~/.bashrc` (where `make install` puts the `eval` line). Add `[ -f ~/.bashrc ] && . ~/.bashrc` to `~/.bash_profile` instead of copying the `eval` line there. |
| zsh: nothing happens on TAB | `print $_comps[docker]` should print `_autocomplete`. If not, the `eval "$(autocomplete zsh)"` line didn't run, or a later `compdef`/plugin manager overrode it; put the line at the end of `~/.zshrc`. |
| A new spec isn't picked up | Re-run `eval "$(autocomplete bash)"`; bash only registers commands at startup. |
| A spec seems to be ignored | `autocomplete check path/to/spec.yaml` shows errors with line numbers. `AUTOCOMPLETE_DEBUG=1` prints errors while completing. |
| A bundled spec behaves like an old version after upgrading | Old installs put specs directly in `share/autocomplete`; those files take priority over the topic folders. Delete the top-level files (`find /usr/local/share/autocomplete -maxdepth 1 -type f -delete`) and run `make install` again. |
| No containers / images suggested | The Docker daemon must be running. |
| List order differs between terminals (📌 snippets not first, `📌 vars` / `-📌` / `🧩` entries mixed in instead of last) | bash sorts the list using your locale. With `LANG=en_US.UTF-8` (VS Code's terminal sets it) macOS ignores emoji when sorting, so entries sort by their text; without `LANG` (C locale) they sort by bytes and emoji come last, 📌 before 🔥. Only the order changes; completion works the same. For the byte order: `export LC_COLLATE=C`. |
| `source <(autocomplete bash)` does nothing | bash 3.2 bug; use `eval "$(autocomplete bash)"`. |

See also [Cache](cache.md): `AUTOCOMPLETE_NOCACHE=1` rules out a stale cache.

---

<!-- docs/how-it-works.md -->

# How it works

`autocomplete bash` prints one `complete -C` line that registers `autocomplete _complete`
for every command that has a spec; no shell function is defined. `autocomplete bash --man`
also registers every `$PATH` command with a section 1 or 8 man page, skipping commands that
already have a completion (bash-completion, Homebrew scripts loaded earlier) and those with
a spec. For such a command the first TAB parses its man page (`man -P cat`, never running
the command itself) into a spec and caches it; a page without options leaves plain filename
completion. When you press TAB, bash
runs `autocomplete _complete` with the line and cursor position in `COMP_LINE` and
`COMP_POINT`. The binary splits the line into words and walks the spec. It
then prints the matching suggestions, already escaped for the shell and trimmed the way
bash expects.

In zsh, `autocomplete zsh` defines one function, `_autocomplete`, and registers it with
`compdef`. On TAB it rebuilds the line up to the cursor from `$words` and `$PREFIX`, then runs
`autocomplete _complete` with `AUTOCOMPLETE_SHELL=zsh`. The engine walks the same spec,
but skips the readline workarounds described below: no folding, no padding for bash's
list, and no trimming at wordbreak characters, because zsh replaces the whole word. It prints
groups of `text<TAB>display` lines that the function passes to `compadd`. Mixed kinds (make
targets and variables) become zsh group headers instead of `[kind]` tags.

bash 3.2 lacks `compopt` and `mapfile`, so nothing here relies on them. Commands are
registered with `complete -o nospace`, and the binary adds the trailing space itself to
finished words. `-o bashdefault` lets bash's own `$VAR` completion handle words starting with `$` (the binary prints nothing for them), so unexported shell variables are listed too. Inside braces the engine completes the name itself (`${COL<TAB>` → `${COLUMNS`, without the `}` bash would add). The init line passes the shell's variable names (`compgen -v`, unexported ones included) to the binary on each TAB. TAB on a complete name lists `}` and the operators. Once an operator follows the name inside braces (`${str%`, `${str:`, `${s//`, `${#`, `${!`), the engine lists the matching bash 3.2 parameter-expansion forms with an example and a short description. The list is display-only: TAB never changes the line, and the values are not known (unexported variables never reach the binary). The same applies to `@` directly after non-space text (`user@<TAB>`): bash's own hostname completion lists hosts. A bare `@` at the start of a word is not handed over; it stays with the engine (spec snippets, `curl @<TAB>`).

Descriptions use the way bash handles several matches: it inserts only their common
prefix and lists the rest. When more than one command matches, the binary returns each
one as `name  -- description`, padded so bash lists one per line. The names differ before
the padding starts, so the descriptions are only displayed, never typed into the command
line. A single match is returned as the bare name. bash 3.2 shows escape codes literally
(`^[[2m`), so the list can't use color.

---

<!-- docs/cache.md -->

# Cache

Specs are read straight from their YAML on every TAB; even the largest bundled ones (about
80 KB) take about 6 ms per TAB, mostly starting the program. The caches below keep the results
of slow work: generating specs from man pages and running commands.

## Why specs aren't cached or compressed

Earlier versions compiled big specs into a binary cache. Measured on a MacBook it made no
difference: a TAB took about 5 ms with or without it, and the largest bundled specs (gh, npm,
about 80 KB) take about 6 ms, nearly all of it starting the program. So it was removed.

Compressing specs (gzip) wouldn't help either. After the first TAB the file is in the OS file
cache, so reading it costs microseconds; decompressing would only add work and an external
library. Shell startup doesn't read specs at all: `autocomplete bash` only lists their names.

## Man page specs

With `eval "$(autocomplete bash --man)"`, commands without a spec get one generated from
their man page on the first TAB (about 0.15 s), stored in `~/.cache/autocomplete/man/<command>.yaml`.
A page that lists no options leaves an empty file, so it isn't parsed again. It is
regenerated when the command's executable or the `autocomplete` binary (a parser update) is newer. To fix up a generated spec, copy it to
`~/.config/autocomplete/` (or run `autocomplete add --from man <command>`): specs there win.

## exec output

An `exec` value with `cache: SECONDS` keeps its output in `~/.cache/autocomplete/exec/` and
reuses it for that long. The entry is per command and current directory (and per typed word
if the command reads `$AUTOCOMPLETE_CUR`). Delete the directory to refresh right away;
`AUTOCOMPLETE_NOCACHE=1` turns it off.

## mvn test names

`mvn test -Dtest=<TAB>` (and `-Dit.test=`) scans `src/test` for test classes and methods, which
can take seconds in big projects. The results are saved in `~/.cache/autocomplete/commands/mvn/` (per
project directory) and reused until a file under any `src/test` directory changes (added,
edited or deleted), or for 1 hour at most. A test module added since the last scan only shows up
after that hour; delete the directory to rescan right away. `AUTOCOMPLETE_NOCACHE` doesn't affect
this cache.

## java main classes

`java <TAB>` lists the `*.java` files under the current directory that declare `main(`;
`mvn exec:java -Dexec.mainClass=<TAB>` offers the same files under `src/main/java` or `src/test/java`
as class names (`com.example.App`). The list is saved in `~/.cache/autocomplete/commands/java/` (per project directory) and reused until a `.java`
file is edited, added, deleted or renamed, or for 1 hour at most. Delete the directory to rescan
right away. `AUTOCOMPLETE_NOCACHE` doesn't affect this cache.
